title: When a 'Candidate' Texting You Is Actually a Bot
hook: Campaigns have always texted voters. Now some of those texts are AI-generated conversations trained to sound like the candidate — personalized, responsive, and not always clearly labeled.
key_points: Political campaigns have long used mass texting to reach voters; what's new is AI generating personalized, back-and-forth conversations rather than a single canned message.
These bots are trained to sound like a specific candidate, adapting replies to what a voter writes back.
Existing rules on political texting (like consent and opt-out requirements) were written for human-sent or scripted messages, not adaptive AI conversations.
Ethical concerns center on disclosure: whether voters are told they're talking to a bot, and how their replies and data get used.
The same underlying tension as other AI-in-politics debates: a genuinely useful outreach tool can also be a more convincing vector for manipulation if it isn't transparent.
content_html: Getting a text from a campaign is nothing new. What's changed is what's on the other end of it: some campaigns now deploy AI trained to sound like the candidate, holding a personalized, responsive conversation with a voter rather than sending one fixed message to everyone.
extra_html: NPR's Maham Javaid reports that these bots adapt their replies to what a voter actually writes back, making the outreach feel more like a real conversation than a mass blast — which is exactly what raises the ethical question. Rules built around consent and opt-outs for political texting were written with a human sender or a scripted message in mind, not an AI system generating a live, tailored back-and-forth. The concern isn't that campaigns are talking to voters; it's whether voters know who — or what — they're actually talking to, a version of the disclosure problem that runs through every new AI-in-politics tool. (This card describes AI-driven political text campaigns in general; specific disclosure rules vary by jurisdiction.)

flashcards.prompt: What's new about AI-generated political text messages, compared to older campaign texting?
flashcards.back_html: Older campaign texts were scripted or human-sent; AI-generated texts hold a personalized, adaptive conversation trained to sound like the candidate, responding to whatever the voter writes back.

flashcards.prompt: Why do existing political-texting rules not neatly cover AI conversation bots?

choices.text: Those rules were written assuming a human-sent or fixed scripted message, not an adaptive AI conversation
Political texting has never been regulated in any way
AI-generated texts are automatically illegal under current law

flashcards.explanation_html: The regulatory gap is about fit, not a total absence of rules — consent and opt-out requirements exist, but weren't designed with adaptive AI conversations in mind.

flashcards.prompt: What's the central ethical concern raised about AI campaign texting?

choices.text: Whether voters are clearly told they're conversing with a bot, not a person
Whether campaigns are allowed to text voters at all
Whether AI bots can legally be registered to vote

flashcards.explanation_html: Disclosure and transparency — not the mere existence of the technology — are what critics are raising concerns about.
